subject: Creativity
title: 3M and the Post-it Note: Innovation by Accident
description: A short lesson to help you apply 3M and the Post-it Note: Innovation by Accident.

hook.text: Spencer Silver invented an adhesive that didn't stick properly. His boss called it useless.

buildup.text: Silver's weak adhesive looked useless, but 3M let employees spend 15% of their time chasing odd ideas.

discovery.text: His colleague Art Fry realized the weak glue was perfect for bookmarks that wouldn't damage pages.

twist.text: 3M's first market test flopped — people didn't understand Post-its until they USED them.

climax.text: 3M's innovation culture (15% time, tolerance for failure, cross-pollination) has produced 60,000+ products.

punchline.text: The Post-it was a failed glue that found the perfect problem.

quiz.question: What 3M policy allowed Spencer Silver to keep developing his 'failed' adhesive?
options: 15% of work time for personal projects

details.summary: The Post-it Note resulted from a failed adhesive combined with an employee's personal need for a reusable bookmark. 3M's organizational culture of tolerating productive failure and allowing employees to pursue personal projects turned an accident into a billion-dollar product line.
details.whyItMatters: The Post-it story demonstrates that innovation often emerges from unexpected combinations of existing elements. Organizations that tolerate productive failure and empower employees create conditions for accidental invention.
takeaways: Spencer Silver invented the weak adhesive while trying to create a strong one
Art Fry identified the practical application years later
3M's 15 percent time policy created the conditions for accidental innovation

faq.question: How did the Post-it Note come about?
faq.answer: Spencer Silver invented a weak, reusable adhesive in 1968 while trying to create a super-strong one. For years, nobody saw a use for it. In 1974, Art Fry used it to create bookmarks for his hymnal. The product was not successfully launched until 1980.

faq.question: What was 3M's role in making it happen?
faq.answer: 3M's 15 percent time policy allowed Silver to keep experimenting with his adhesive even though it had no obvious commercial application. The company culture tolerated years of unsuccessful attempts to find a use before Fry's insight finally unlocked its potential.
